title: Water
alt: Three cooling units side by side on a roof, each labelled: an air-cooled chiller sending out only warm air, drawn as red rising lines; a cooling tower with a water basin, sending out warm moist air and water vapour as white puffs, with a light-blue mains water line coming in and a grey line sending some water to the drain; and a hybrid cooler with wet pads at its sides that are wetted only on hot days. Below the roof, bars show the water each uses in a year for the reference layout: none for air-cooled, about 1,900 to 5,300 cubic metres for hybrid coolers, about 15,400 to 42,700 cubic metres for cooling towers.
sources: Yearly water for the reference layout, cooling towers about 15,435 to 42,722 m3 and hybrid (adiabatic) coolers about 1,914 to 5,298 m3: the tool's Cooling and water card (method: evaporation up to about 1.5 L per kWh of heat rejected, blow-down = evaporation / (cycles - 1), US DOE FEMP)

steps.caption: Three ways to throw a data centre’s heat away: an air-cooled chiller, a cooling tower and a hybrid cooler.
An air-cooled chiller sends out only warm air. It uses no water.
A cooling tower cools by evaporating water. Warm, moist air and water vapour rise from it. Mains water replaces what evaporates, and some is sent to the drain to keep the water clean.
A hybrid cooler runs dry, like the air-cooled one, most of the time. On hot days it wets its pads to cool the incoming air, and uses some water.
Water used in a year for the reference layout: none for air-cooled, about 1,900 to 5,300 m³ for hybrid coolers, about 15,400 to 42,700 m³ for cooling towers.
The difference is what each sends out: warm air, or warm air and water.
